title: Wilson Theorem Generalizations for Composite Moduli

problemStatement.formal: For n ≥ 2: (n-1)! ≡ -1 (mod n) iff n prime; (3)! ≡ 2 (mod 4); (n-1)! ≡ 0 (mod n) for composite n > 4. The Gauss-Wilson classification: ∏ units ≡ -1 (mod n) iff n ∈ {4, p^k, 2p^k}.
problemStatement.plain: Complete classification of factorial residues and unit products modulo n, extending Wilson's theorem to all moduli.
whyMatters: Wilson's theorem is a fundamental result in number theory
The Gauss generalization connects to primitive root theory and cyclic group structure
Provides a computational primality test and characterizes the unit group structure

proven: Composite factorial vanishing: n | (n-1)! for composite n > 4
Complete factorial classification for all n ≥ 2
unitsProduct_eq_factorial: bridge between unitsProduct and factorial for primes
unitsProduct_prime: Wilson's theorem in unitsProduct formulation
Square roots of unity analysis and Gauss-Wilson form detection
Gauss-Wilson classification verified computationally for n ≤ 300
isCyclic_units_iff_gaussWilson: Mathlib's cyclic units characterization restated

insights: The Gauss-Wilson classification reduces to: IsCyclic (ZMod n)ˣ ↔ product of units ≡ -1
Mathlib has ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff giving the full cyclic characterization
CRITICAL: ¬IsCyclic G → |{x|x²=1}| ≥ 3 is FALSE for general CommGroup G. Counterexample: Z/3×Z/3 has |{x|x²=1}|=1 but is not cyclic

For (ZMod n)ˣ specifically, the theorem IS true because: (1) n ≥ 3 ensures -1 ≠ 1, so |S| ≥ 2; (2) ¬IsCyclic means n decomposes via CRT into factors each contributing independent 2-torsion, giving |S| ≥ 4
Two-involution trick is cleaner than three-involution trick: uses prod_involution_const directly, no transversal needed
Z/3×Z/3 counterexample: |{x|x²=1}| = 1 (only identity), group order 9, not cyclic, but 2-torsion is trivial because group has odd order
For abelian groups with even order and ¬IsCyclic, the 2-Sylow has rank ≥ 2 giving |{x|x²=1}| ≥ 4
isCyclic_of_card_pow_eq_one_le needs ALL n, not just n=2, so the contrapositive alone doesn't suffice

approaches.name: Two-involution trick (via prod_involution_const)
approaches.description: Use FPF involution x↦cx with c²=1, c≠1 to show ∏S = c^(|S|/2). Two such involutions give d^(|S|/2)=1 and c^(|S|/2)=1, so ∏S=1. Requires |S|≥3.

approaches.name: CRT decomposition for 2-torsion bound
approaches.description: For ¬IsCyclic (ZMod n)ˣ, use ZMod.chineseRemainder to decompose into coprime factors, each contributing independent 2-torsion, proving |S|≥4.
